nameStory: Hamilton's spindle gets its name from Francis Buchanan-Hamilton, a Scottish botanist who explored the plant life of India and Nepal in the early 1800s. The "spindle" part comes from the hard wood of these plants, which was traditionally used to make spindles for spinning thread. It's also called Himalayan spindle, hinting at its mountain origins in Asia.
description: Hamilton's spindle is a deciduous shrub or small tree that can grow 10-20 feet tall, originally from the mountains of Asia but now planted in New England gardens. It has a rounded, spreading shape with smooth-edged oval leaves that turn beautiful shades of yellow, orange, and red in fall. The plant produces small greenish-white flowers in spring, followed by distinctive pink or red capsule fruits that split open to reveal bright orange seeds dangling on threads.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Four-lobed pink to red capsules about the size of a small marble split open in fall to reveal bright orange seeds hanging on thin threads like tiny ornaments

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves 2-5 inches long with smooth edges and pointed tips, arranged in opposite pairs along the stems, turning brilliant yellow-orange-red in fall

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small greenish-white flowers with 4 petals appear in flat-topped clusters in late spring, not showy but numerous

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright shrub or small tree with a rounded crown, multiple stems from the base, and smooth gray-brown bark

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Small, pointed winter buds pressed close to the twig with overlapping scales, green to reddish-brown

habitat: In New England, Hamilton's spindle is found primarily in cultivated landscapes, botanical gardens, and residential plantings as an ornamental shrub. It prefers well-drained soil and can tolerate both sun and partial shade. Since it's not native, you won't find it naturalized in wild areas, but it thrives in suburban settings and managed landscapes.

seasonality.spring: Small greenish-white flowers appear in late spring in flat clusters, not particularly showy but numerous. New leaves emerge bright green and smooth-edged.
seasonality.summer: The plant is in full leaf with dense, green foliage providing good screening. Flowers develop into small green fruits that gradually enlarge through the summer.
seasonality.fall: This is showtime - leaves turn spectacular shades of yellow, orange, and red while the pink-red capsule fruits split open to reveal dangling orange seeds.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the plant's structure, with small pointed buds and sometimes persistent fruit remnants. The smooth bark and branching pattern become visible.

funFact: The bright orange seeds dangle from the split-open fruits on silk-like threads, creating what looks like tiny Chinese lanterns swaying in the breeze - this dramatic display evolved to catch the attention of birds who eat the seeds and spread them to new locations.
confusionNotes: Hamilton's spindle can be confused with other euonymus species, especially burning bush (winged euonymus), but Hamilton's spindle lacks the corky "wings" on its stems that give burning bush its distinctive appearance. The four-lobed fruits and dangling orange seeds are the giveaway - remember "Hamilton's hanging seeds" to keep them straight.
contextualKnowledge: While Hamilton's spindle isn't invasive like its notorious relative burning bush, gardeners should be aware that birds can spread the seeds, potentially establishing new plants beyond where they're planted. The name "spindle tree" applies to many species in this genus, all referring to their historically important hard wood.
compareHints: Among New England's euonymus species, Hamilton's spindle stands out for its four-lobed pink fruits and dangling orange seeds on threads. Burning bush has similar fall color but distinctive corky wing-like ridges on its stems, while wintercreeper is a low-growing vine rather than an upright shrub. The threadlike seed attachments are Hamilton's spindle's signature feature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Euonymus relatives in New England, winged euonymus is the only one with prominent corky wings on the stems.
Unlike winged euonymus (burning bush) which is deciduous with prominent corky wing-like ridges on stems, Fortune's spindle stays evergreen and has smooth, round stems.
Unlike its notorious relative winged euonymus (burning bush), European spindle lacks the prominent corky 'wings' on its stems and has much less intense fall leaf color.
American wahoo differs from its cousin winged euonymus (burning bush) by lacking the distinctive corky wings on its stems and being much less common.

Large-leaved spindle stands out from its New England relatives primarily by leaf size – its leaves are significantly larger than the small leaves of winged euonymus or the narrow leaves of other spindle species.
Unlike its deciduous relatives like winged euonymus (burning bush) or wahoo, Japanese spindle keeps its leaves year-round.
